diagnostic_approaches.name: Thoracic ultrasound prior to chest tube insertion
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify key thoracic structures and sonographic signs before insertion
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Utilize ultrasound to identify important structures, lung sliding, lung point, diaphragm, or pleural based tumors prior to insertion
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When time permits prior to insertion
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: utilizing ultrasound to identify important structures, lung sliding, lung point, diaphragm, or pleural based tumors prior to the insertion of the chest tube

diagnostic_approaches.name: Digital palpation to verify pleural space entry
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm entry into the pleural space during insertion
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Perform circumferential digital palpation with the index finger or the fifth "pinky" finger
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A digital palpation is then performed circumferentially with the index ﬁnger or some instance or the ﬁfth “pinky” ﬁnger (Fig. 3d).

diagnostic_approaches.name: Aspiration of air or fluid to confirm placement
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm proper placement in the pleural space
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: During anesthetic, aspirate air or fluid via the needle/syringe
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: If no fluid nor air can be aspirated, reconfirming position with ultrasound can be invaluable
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: During the anesthetic process, either air or ﬂuid should be aspirated to conﬁrm proper placement.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest X-ray verification of tube position
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Verify proper chest tube position radiographically
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Obtain a chest x-ray to confirm tube position
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Proper tube position verified on chest x-ray; timing can be at procedure end
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Also acceptable at the conclusion of the procedure
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Verify proper tube position with a chest x-ray (also acceptable at the conclusion of the procedure)

diagnostic_approaches.name: Functional assessment of chest tube patency (fogging and fluid fluctuation)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess chest tube function after insertion
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Observe fogging with expiration and visualize fluctuation of fluid in collection container
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Fogging indicates air drainage; fluid fluctuation indicates patency
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Draining air from the tube will fog with expiration. The patency of the tube can be assessed by visualizing ﬂuctuation of the ﬂuid in the collection container.

diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Define anatomical landmarks for a safe insertion zone
criteria_or_scoring: anterior border of the latissimus dorsi
lateral border of the pectoralis major muscle
a line superior to the horizontal level of the nipple (or superior to the submammary fold)
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Identify the borders of latissimus dorsi and pectoralis major and stay superior to nipple/submammary fold
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The safety triangle is deﬁne as the anterior border of the latissimus dorsi, the lateral border of the pectoralis major muscle,

diagnostic_approaches.name: Definition of large-bore chest tube (French size threshold)
criteria_or_scoring: Most authors define large bore chest tubes as ≥20 French
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Most authors deﬁne large bore chest tubes as ≥20 French

diagnostic_approaches.name: French size conversion to millimeters for chest tubes
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Convert French size to outer diameter in mm
criteria_or_scoring: French (F) equals outer diameter multiplied by 0.333
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Where French (F) is a measurement of outer diameter of the chest tube multiplied by 0.333—thus a 24 F is 8 mm, and 12 F is 4 mm.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Anatomic landmarking for insertion site (3–5th ICS, mid-axillary line)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Select preferred insertion site within safe triangle
criteria_or_scoring: 3–5th Intercostal space within the mid axillary line is preferred
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Identify 3–5th intercostal space at mid-axillary line within the safe triangle
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The 3–5th Intercostal space within the mid axillary line is the preferred position well within the “safe” triangle

diagnostic_approaches.name: Clamping trial to determine air leak before chest tube removal
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Determine presence of an air leak prior to chest tube removal.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Clamping trials are commonly perform prior to removal of a chest tube placed for pneumothorax.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Presence or absence of an air leak during a clamping trial.
limitations: some experts would never clamp to determine an air leak.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Prior to removal of a chest tube placed for pneumothorax.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Clamping trials are commonly perform prior to removal of a chest tube placed for pneumothorax.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Digital drain device air leak measurement
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Objective measurement of air leak to facilitate chest tube removal.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: If no leak is measured, removal may be hastened.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When evaluating for chest tube removal.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: new digital drain devices may hasten chest tube removal if no leak is measured instead of the more subjective visual “bubble” detection method [28].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Visual 'bubble' detection method for air leak
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Subjective visual detection of air leaks.
limitations: Difficulty determining whether small visual leaks/'bubbles' are truly present
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The controversy arises from the ability to determine whether small visual leaks/“bubbles” are truly present.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Radiographic evaluation for chest tube side-hole (malposition check)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Investigate tube position when subcutaneous emphysema develops.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Visualize side hole on X-ray or CT imaging.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Often a side hole can often be visualized on X-ray or CT imaging.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Thoracic ultrasound to identify diaphragm and surrounding structures
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Determine depth and location of surrounding organs/structures and demonstrate the diaphragm.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use ultrasound to determine depth and location of surrounding organs/structures.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: recognizing anatomy especially with an ultrasound to determine depth and location of surrounding organs/structures.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest X-ray interpretation pitfall: high-riding diaphragm vs pleural fluid
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: The high-riding diaphragm can often be mistaken for fluid on CXR.
limitations: Risk of misinterpreting high-riding diaphragm as pleural fluid.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When interpreting CXR for pleural effusion.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The high-riding diaphragm can often be mistaken for ﬂuid in a patient with atelectasis or a small amount of pleural effusion on CXR.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest tube output thresholds for suspected intercostal artery bleeding
criteria_or_scoring: greater than 1500 mL in a 24-h period
persistent bleeding of 150–200 mL/h for 2–4 h
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Monitor chest tube output volumes over time.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Consider consultation with thoracic surgery and/or interventional radiology when thresholds are met.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: with greater than 1500 mL in a 24-h period or persistent bleeding of 150–200 mL/h for 2–4 h [33].

treatment_algorithms.title: Large bore chest tube surgical/blunt dissection technique algorithm
treatment_algorithms.condition: Chest tube insertion for pneumothorax or pleural fluid drainage
specific_recommendations: Attach the tube to a pleural drainage system—generally -20 cm H2O for fluid to water seal for pneumothoraces (unless unable to keep up with the evacuation of air).
decision_points_and_pathways: The “Safe Triangle” is the preferred location.
Guiding the tube anterior cranially for pneumothorax or posterior caudally for fluid is the general approach.
If no fluid nor air can be aspirated, reconfirming position with ultrasound can be invaluable.
Very little resistance should be felt, upon insertion. If significant resistance is felt or kinking is visualized—then tube has demonstrated a false path outside the chest wall cavity.
contraindications_and_exceptions: There are no absolute contraindications to chest tube placement in the setting of an emergency.
Relative contraindications include coagulopathies, pleural adhesions, loculated effusions, high riding diaphragms, or trauma with displacement of intraabdominal organs into the thoracic cavity.
monitoring_requirements: Verify proper tube position with a chest x-ray (also acceptable at the conclusion of the procedure).
The patency of the tube can be assessed by visualizing fluctuation of the fluid in the collection container.
alternative_approaches: Seldinger technique; some companies do provide large bore chest tubes that can be placed by this method.
Trocar method (otherwise known as the “harpoon”) which is discouraged.
treatment_algorithms.source_excerpt: Attach the tube to a pleural drainage system—generally -20 cm H2O for ﬂuid to water seal for pneumothoraces (unless unable to keep up with the evacuation of air).

clinical_guidelines.title: ACCP Delphi consensus (2001) recommendations for asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax
specific_recommendations: Use either a small-bore catheter (≤14 F) or 16–22 F for an asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP).
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: recommend using either a small-bore catheter (≤14 F) or 16–22 F for an asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP)

clinical_guidelines.title: ACCP recommendations for chest tube sizing in larger/unstable pneumothorax and anticipated BPF
clinical_guidelines.condition: Pneumothorax with clinical instability; anticipated bronchopleural fistula
specific_recommendations: Chest tube size 16–22 F in the setting of a larger pneumothoraces with clinically instability.
Use a 24–28 F standard chest tube in the case of an anticipated bronchopleural fistula (BPF).
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: larger pneumothoraces with clinically instability; anticipated bronchopleural fistula (BPF)
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The ACCP consensus group makes the case for chest tube size 16–22 F in the setting of a larger pneumothoraces with clinically instability or a 24–28 F standard chest tube

clinical_guidelines.title: British Thoracic Society guidelines for spontaneous pneumothorax management
specific_recommendations: Allow observation regardless of size in the asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Provide a pathway for simple aspiration versus small bore chest tube for the symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax or secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.
decision_points_and_pathways: Observation regardless of size in the asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Simple aspiration versus small bore chest tube pathway for symptomatic primary or secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax; symptomatic primary or secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: allowing for observation regardless of size in the asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax, and even has a pathway for simple aspiration versus small bore chest tube

clinical_guidelines.title: ATLS recommendation for chest tube size in hemothorax
specific_recommendations: Use a 28–32 F chest tube for management of hemothorax.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) supporting a 28–32 F chest tube for management of hemothorax

clinical_guidelines.title: Postthoracotomy pleural drain size recommendation
specific_recommendations: Use a 19–24 F pleural drain after thoracotomy.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: recent recommendation suggests a 19–24 F pleural drain

clinical_guidelines.title: Trocar Method Discouragement
specific_recommendations: This technique is discouraged [20, 21].
We also generally avoid the use of the sharp metal trocar for insertion given its ability to cause penetrating trauma.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: avoid the use of the sharp metal trocar
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: the blunt dissection technique offers several advantages over the Seldinger techniques
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Trocar Method This technique is discouraged [20, 21].

clinical_guidelines.title: ACCP Consensus on Clamping Trials for Spontaneous Pneumothorax
specific_recommendations: Clamping trials are commonly perform prior to removal of a chest tube placed for pneumothorax.
53% of then panel of experts would never clamp a chest tube to determine the presence of and air leak [7].

clinical_guidelines.title: Heimlich Valve Outpatient Management Criteria for Persistent Air Leaks
clinical_guidelines.condition: Postoperative air leak management on water seal
specific_recommendations: Many postoperative patients with air leaks who are tolerating water seal can be managed with a Heimlich valve
They discharged patients with persistent air leaks and scheduled follow-up visits as long as certain criteria were met
(1) asymptomatic, (2) no subcutaneous emphysema after 14 days of portable device, and (3) the pleural space have not increased in size [29].

no subcutaneous emphysema after 14 days of portable device
the pleural space have not increased in size

clinical_guidelines.title: Chest Tube Removal Thresholds for Pleural Effusion
clinical_guidelines.condition: Pleural effusion (criteria for chest tube removal)
specific_recommendations: there again remains no consensus and a large discrepancy ranging from less than 100 cc/24 h to <500 cc/24 h depending on the cause of the pleural effusion [30].
decision_points_and_pathways: less than 100 cc/24 h
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: rate of pleural fluid drainage (cc/24 h)
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: ranging from less than 100 cc/24 h to <500 cc/24 h depending on the cause of the pleural effusion [30].

clinical_guidelines.title: Drain Removal Thresholds After Lung Resection
clinical_guidelines.condition: Postthoracic lung resection chest tube management
specific_recommendations: removing chest tube based on a weight-based approach of <5 mL/kg/24 h compared to <200 mL/24 h, showed almost no difference [31].
decision_points_and_pathways: <5 mL/kg/24 h
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: daily drainage volume (mL/kg/24 h or mL/24 h)
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: weight-based approach vs fixed 200 mL/24 h threshold
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Postthoracic lung resection, removing chest tube based on a weight-based approach of <5 mL/kg/24 h compared to <200 mL/24 h, showed almost no difference [31].

clinical_guidelines.condition: Empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion (chest tube removal)
specific_recommendations: some authors recommending removal when the fluid becomes more clear and drainage is <50 cc/24 h [32].
decision_points_and_pathways: fluid becomes more clear
drainage is <50 cc/24 h

clinical_guidelines.title: Technique for Safe Chest Tube Removal
specific_recommendations: Removing the chest tube is done quickly and with intention while the patient is demonstrating positive intrathoracic pressure (usually done by an audible humming).
if deciding to remove the chest tube on the ventilator, this would be done during an inspiratory hold ... when the intrathoracic pressure is positive.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: this would be done during an inspiratory hold (seemingly counterintuitively) when the intrathoracic pressure is positive.

clinical_guidelines.title: Preventing Injury During Chest Tube Insertion
specific_recommendations: recognizing anatomy especially with an ultrasound to determine depth and location of surrounding organs/structures.
we find demonstrating the diaphragm of the utmost importance to avoid a subdiaphragmatic injury to the liver or spleen.
We also generally avoid the use of the sharp metal trocar for insertion given its ability to cause penetrating trauma.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: avoid the use of the sharp metal trocar
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: ultrasound to determine depth and location

clinical_guidelines.title: Bleeding Thresholds Prompting Surgical/IR Consultation
clinical_guidelines.condition: Suspected intercostal artery bleeding after chest tube placement
specific_recommendations: Considerations for consultation with thoracic surgery and/or interventional radiology for suspected intercostal artery bleeding with greater than 1500 mL in a 24-h period or persistent bleeding of 150–200 mL/h for 2–4 h [33].
decision_points_and_pathways: greater than 1500 mL in a 24-h period
persistent bleeding of 150–200 mL/h for 2–4 h

clinical_guidelines.title: Management of Subcutaneous Emphysema and Parenchymal Injury
specific_recommendations: Development of marked subcutaneous emphysema should warrant an investigation of the tube.
In direct parenchymal injury, discussions with thoracic surgery are in order as surgical revision may be considered.
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: investigation of the tube when marked subcutaneous emphysema develops
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Development of marked subcutaneous emphysema should warrant an investigation of the tube.

clinical_guidelines.title: Wound Infection/Empyema Prevention and Management
specific_recommendations: Proper insertion technique can reduce wound infections; however, prolonged tubes can lead to infection.
Active surveillance and early antibiosis can improve outcomes as well as ensuring tube patency.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Active surveillance and early antibiosis can improve outcomes as well as ensuring tube patency.

clinical_guidelines.title: Prevention of Reexpansion Pulmonary Edema During Drainage
clinical_guidelines.condition: Reexpansion pulmonary edema risk with chest drainage
specific_recommendations: Most authors recommend reducing expiratory pressures less than -20 cm H2O can prevent this from occurring and stopping chest drainage at signs of chest pressure to reduce the exaggerated negative intrathoracic pressure.
decision_points_and_pathways: reduce expiratory pressures less than -20 cm H2O
stop chest drainage at signs of chest pressure
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: monitor for signs of chest pressure
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: reducing expiratory pressures less than -20 cm H2O can prevent this from occurring and stopping chest drainage at signs of chest pressure

clinical_guidelines.title: Postprocedure Pain Control With NSAIDs or Opioids
clinical_guidelines.condition: Pain management after chest tube placement
specific_recommendations: For postprocedure pain, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and opioids can be used for pain control.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: For postprocedure pain, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and opioids can be used for pain control.

clinical_guidelines.title: Analgesia and Nerve Block for Refractory Pain
specific_recommendations: Local anesthetic or in some cases an intercostal nerve block could be used for refractory pain when the tube is still needed.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Local anesthetic or in some cases an intercostal nerve block could be used for refractory pain when the tube is still needed.
